doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

chapter: Producers, Chick's legacy and the music business
title: Streaming and the changing music business
summary: Kirsh's views on decentralized recording, streaming and musicians' pay.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Indeed. It looks like it’s doing well with streams and so forth.
Streams, right. Yeah. The new world.
Whoever knew that we would use the word “stream” in regards to music.
Yes. I mean streaming, streaming, streaming — musicians still aren’t getting paid. You know?
What is your general — to sort of wrap up — do you have a general opinion about the music industry the way it’s recorded, the way it’s delivered, the way it’s not paid for? Or just things in general?

Well the music business has changed. It’s become a real decentralized — in terms of recording of course, it’s decentralized. And there’s good and bad. I mean what you have now is the ability of any artist to create recordings that he would like to do, any projects he would like to do because in your own home you have a recording studio. So that part is good. The difficult part is getting people to hear it. And in that respect streaming services are a definite advantage to getting works out. You know there are probably, of course the record company which is a marketing arm to use. But if you can’t actually work with a record company then streaming is an outlet, aside from direct marketing, that you want to do on your own. I don’t know how much musicians want to do that and so forth. So I’m not sure, you mean in terms of direction?
The way that music is created and delivered I think you pretty much answered my question.
Okay. Yeah I know, it’s a different time. In some ways better. I always enjoy a roomful of musicians, people having fun and just making something together. So that’s my vote.
